newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Portugal appeals as gateway for car exports.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Portugal appeals as gateway for car exports.

text.p: Car and component manufacturers are expanding production in Portugal which they are using as a gateway for exports to Europe and the Americas.
Manufacturers setting up in Portugal benefit from generous state incentives, a skilled work force, strategic location and stable political and economic scene, industry officials say.

The latest project was announced last month when Avon Automotive, a division of British tyre manufacturer Avon Rubber PLC, opened a factory in northern Portugal to produce automotive hoses for Ford plants in Spain and Brazil.
The factory in Tondela near the city of Viseu will involve an initial $5.2 million investment that is expected to increase over the next year with the creation of up to 100 jobs.

"We decided that Portugal was one of the places where the automotive industry was going to grow substantially over the next year," spokesman Gordon Morris told Reuters from Avon Rubber's head office in Bradford-on-Avon in central England.
"We are certain that other European car manufacturers will set up in Iberia," he added.
Several car manufacturers including Ford, Volkswagen, Renault, Opel and Seat now produce cars in Portugal.
The biggest foreign investment in Portugal is the AutoEuropa joint venture between Ford and Volkswagen, launched in April 1995 at Palmela, 30 miles (50 km) south of Lisbon.
AutoEuropa expects to boost its output of passenger vans by some 20 percent to 121,000 vehicles in 1996, a spokeswoman said. Its main markets are Germany, Britain and France.

Asked why Portugal was chosen as the site for AutoEuropa, its managing director Ralph Rosignolo told Reuters: "We looked for a country where industry had a spirit of cooperation with the government, and where the government was stable.
"Portugal has a stable and cooperative government."
He added: "We also searched for a country with a work force capable of satisfying our needs: young, aggressive and able to learn our working techniques.
"We looked for strong infrastructure. The road system, harbours and railway network had to satisfy our needs. For us, Portugal represented the perfect combination of all these."
Rosignolo said the Socialist government had awarded tax and training incentives to AutoEuropa, but he gave no details.

In June this year French carmaker Renault said it planned to hand over a car assembly plant in central Portugal to the Portuguese government, but said it would maintain a long term commercial and industrial presence in Portugal.

Renault drew strong criticism from Portugal when it said it would close the plant in Setubal, which produces Clio cars, at the end of last year because of the poor performance of the southern European car market.

The government, which owned 30 percent of the plant, said it would press on with a lawsuit lodged by the previous Social Democrat government claiming 53 billion escudos ($340 million) in compensation over the closure plans.

But in June the government announced that it had dropped the lawsuit and agreed a deal with Renault. It said a state company would take over control of the factory, which will continue producing Clios until July 31, 1998.
Renault said it would remain active in Portugal.
"Renault plans to maintain a strong, competitive industrial and commercial presence in Portugal," Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said in Lisbon in June.

In February this year the Portuguese cabinet gave the green light to General Motors to expand its operations in central Portugal and build two new models of Opel vehicles for an investment of 14.5 billion escudos ($95 million).
Ford was considering new investment possibilities in Portugal, spokesman Artur Lemos said. He declined to give details.
Diario Economico newspaper said in September that Ford was considering a possible joint venture with the South Korean Halla Group to build a car components factory in Portugal.
The paper said the Socialist government was considering providing financial and tax incentives for the project.
"Portugal has a key role in Ford's investment strategy," Lemos told Reuters.
He praised the quality of the Portuguese work force and said Ford viewed Portugal as a place to invest primarily for export production as its domestic market was too small.
Portugal was well-placed to supply cars and parts to the rest of Europe as it was a signatory of the border-free Schengen agreement.
Portugal's position along the Atlantic coast meant it was well-located to serve the Americas.
Portugal's stable political environment and progress in meeting the tough entry test for joining a European single currency in 1999 made it an appealing choice for investment, Lemos said.
